method: Verdicts compared from result.json at HEAD (this swarm) and origin/main (the collaborator swarm). No file was merged or modified to make this comparison.

ours.hypothesis: If Darwin's denudation argument holds, the time elapsed since the latter part of the Secondary (Mesozoic) period, i.e. since the youngest Chalk, is roughly 300 million years or more on the modern radiometrically calibrated timescale.
ours.passCriterion: Pre-registered. measured.unit: Ma, age of the top of the Maastrichtian (end of the Chalk); Darwin's figure was 306.7 million years
measured.uncertainty: ICS boundary ages for these stages carry uncertainties of about 0.2 Ma, far below the threshold

theirs.passCriterion: The age of the Cretaceous-Paleogene (Mesozoic-Cenozoic) boundary in the current International Chronostratigraphic Chart, as served by Macrostrat and cross-checked against the Paleobiology Database timescale, is >= 300 Ma; equivalently the maximum possible duration of post-Chalk denudation (time since the youngest Chalk) is >= 300 Myr.

measured.unit: Ma (age of the top of the Cretaceous / Mesozoic = end of Chalk deposition)
measured.uncertainty: all 7 readings agree to within 0 Myr; ICS quotes no error bar on the K/Pg boundary age

ours.passCriterion: Pre-registered. Criterion A (long-lasting cold states): with d18O linearly interpo

measured.unit: fraction of the last 2.6 Myr with benthic d18O >= 4.0 per mil (pre-registered threshold 0.20)
measured.uncertainty: LR04 standard errors are 0.03-0.1 per mil per point, small relative to the 4.0 threshold

ours.hypothesis: If weight varies as the cube of a linear dimension during growth, then across childhood and adolescence the population mean body weight scales with the population mean stature with a log-log exponent near 3, so the weight-for-age curve is approximately the cube of the stature-for-age curve.
ours.passCriterion: Pre-registered. Data: US NHANES examination data, cycles 2013-2014, 2015-2016 and 2017-2018 (Body Measures BMX_H/I/J and Demographics DEMO_H/I/J XPT files), examined participants aged 2 to 19 years with measured standing height (BMXHT, cm) and weight (BMXWT, kg). For each sex, compute MEC-exam-weighted (WTMEC2YR) mean height and mean weight in 1-year age bins (18 bins), regress log(mean weight) on

measured.unit: log-log exponent of mean weight on mean height across ages 2-19, males (pre-registered band 2.5-3.5); females given in extra
measured.n: 4905 males and 4810 females in 18 age bins each

theirs.hypothesis: Across human growth, body weight scales approximately as the cube of stature (log-log slope near 3), and cubing the stature-versus-age curve removes most of the difference in shape between the stature curve and the weight curve.
theirs.passCriterion: Pre-registered, on pooled NHANES 2007-2018 individuals aged 0-19.99 yr with measured weight and stature (recumbent length < 24 months, standing height >= 24 months), sexes pooled with sex-specific values reported. (1) Cube tendency: the OLS slope b of log10(weight) on log10(stature) over all individuals satisfies 2.5 <= b <= 3.5 (95% CI reported; reduced-major-axis slope reported as sensitivity),

measured.unit: log-log OLS exponent of weight on stature, individuals aged 0-19

ours.hypothesis: If chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen, with few below six and fewer still above sixteen, then across plant species the haploid (gametic) number n has most of its mass in 6 <= n <= 16, a small lower tail (n < 6) and a still smaller upper tail (n > 16).
ours.passCriterion: Pre-registered. Data: the Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB, Rice et al. 2015), 'statistics' API output (one row per resolved species name with the median gametophytic/sporophytic counts) retrieved per major group (Angiosperms, Gymnosperms, Pteridophytes, Bryophytes) in CSV. One n per species: the median resolved gametophytic count; where only a sporophytic (2n) count is given, n = 2n/2; species wi

measured.unit: share of plant species with haploid number n > 16 (claim: 'fewer still' than the share with n < 6, which is given in extra)
measured.uncertainty: binomial standard error below 0.002 at this sample size

theirs.hypothesis: Across plant and animal species, the gametic (haploid) chromosome number n lies mostly between 6 and 16: the fraction of taxa with n < 6 is small and the fraction with n > 16 is smaller still.
theirs.passCriterion: Pre-registered. Plants: species-level gametic numbers from the Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB) statistics service for all four major groups (Angiosperms, Gymnosperms, Pteridophytes, Bryophytes), using each species' median parsed n. Animals: the Animal Chromosome Count Database (ACC) table (haploid N where given, else 2N/2), one median value per species. For each kingdom compute f_low = fraction

measured.unit: fraction of animal genera with haploid n > 16 (plant genera: 0.320); fraction with n < 6: animals 0.080, plants 0.011
measured.uncertainty: database census; genus-level n = 8414 plant and 5285 animal genera, species-level n = 64926 and 12221

ours.passCriterion: Pre-registered. Per vertebra, relative spine height h = (neural spine apex to centrum reference distance) / cranial centrum height. Per species: W = mean h over T1-T4 ('withers'); P = mean h over the posterior thoracics T10-T13 (terrestrial trough region); WI = W/P ('withers index'); HI = mean h over the last three lumbars / P ('haunch index'). measured.unit: withers index WI (mean of the two pinniped species); terrestrial carnivoran WI min 1.238, median 1.910

measured.uncertainty: exact one-sided Mann-Whitney U, pinnipeds < terrestrial: W p = 0.0023, WI p = 0.0012 (n = 2 vs 40; smallest attainable p = 0.0012)
